questions.q: How does presenting the incident to the broader engineering team differ from briefing Dana Whitfield and Casey Lindqvist?
options: It's the exact same content and order, delivered to a bigger room
This room already understands Kubernetes scheduling and cluster-wide averages, so Theo doesn't re-explain concepts — the focus is the same honest mechanism plus a clear, specific ask of what changes
The engineering team doesn't need to know the root cause, only the leadership team does
The engineering team presentation skips the follow-up actions entirely
questions.explain: The leadership briefing in Lesson 17 led with business impact for a non-specialist audience; this room already has the technical background, so the presentation can go straight into mechanism and action.

questions.q: What five-part agenda does Theo run for the after-action report?
options: Budget review, headcount, roadmap, Q&A, adjourn
Timeline, root cause, the fix, what went right, follow-up actions
Apology, blame assignment, punishment, reassurance, closing
Sale results, marketing numbers, customer reviews, press coverage, thanks
questions.explain: Theo follows the Lesson 15 report's own structure closely, since this audience is exactly who that structure was built for.

questions.q: What specifically keeps this postmortem blameless, according to the lesson?
options: The word "blameless" printed at the top of the report
How the meeting itself is run — Theo keeps the conversation on the mechanism and the dashboard's design gap, and redirects questions that drift toward "whose fault was this"
Not inviting anyone from the team that built the original Deployment
Skipping the root-cause discussion entirely
questions.explain: A report can claim to be blameless in its wording, but it's the live redirection of blame-seeking questions back toward mechanism that actually enforces a blameless culture in the room.

questions.q: What happens to the Lesson 15 follow-up actions table during this meeting?
options: It's read aloud once and then filed away unchanged
Each row is converted into a tracked ticket live in the meeting, with the owner confirming out loud and able to push back on the due date
It's deleted since the incident is already resolved
It's handed only to Dana Whitfield for safekeeping
questions.explain: Converting the table into tickets with the owner present, able to confirm or adjust the due date, is what keeps follow-up actions from quietly slipping.

questions.q: Why is root cause presented before the fix, rather than after?
options: Order doesn't matter for this kind of meeting
So the room understands why the fix (the real topologySpreadConstraints YAML) was the right one, instead of just being told a change was made
Because the fix is confidential and can't be shown to the whole team
Because the root cause takes longer to explain than the fix
questions.explain: Presenting the mechanism first lets the room evaluate the fix against the actual cause, seeing cause and validation data side by side rather than taking the fix on faith.
